newsitem.title: ITALY: Reverse exodus could be breakthrough, WFP says.
newsitem.headline: Reverse exodus could be breakthrough, WFP says.

text.p: The head of the U.N. food aid agency said on Friday a homeward movement by hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees from eastern Zaire could signal a breakthrough in humanitarian attempts to keep them from starving to death.
"We consider this very significant news," said Catherine Bertini, executive director of the World Food Programme (WFP).
In Zaire, an official of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said several hundred thousand Rwandan Hutu refugees were heading home from eastern Zaire on Friday.

Bertini told reporters at the U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit that between 3,000 and 10,000 people had already crossed the border into Rwanda at Gisenyi and 75,000 others were waiting to move in. They were being checked at the border for weapons.

She said the WFP had pre-positioned food "all along the border" and would be delivering it to refugees. They would receive food whether they remained in border camps in Rwanda or be fed along the way if they kept moving.
The WFP had 750 tonnes -- enough to feed 200,000 people for 10 days -- and could get more to border points within 48 hours.

Bertini said most of the refugees returning were women, children and elderly. "That means that somehow there has been a break between them and the armed guards who have been intimidating them from leaving," she said.
Thousands of armed Hutus -- ex-Rwandan soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen -- had until now prevented ordinary Rwandan refugees from returning home.
Bertini said it was too early to say if the reverse exodus could affect plans for a international force to be sent to the area.

"It's very good news because it's in all our interests to help people to go home and if these people are deciding voluntarily...to go home to Rwanda, we're going to help them get there and get settled as quickly as possible," she said.
The refugees fled into Zaire after the Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis in 1994. Many fear reprisals back home for their role in the slaughter.
